messages.content: We reach the river crossing at dusk. The water is high and brown with silt.
Brennic spits into the reeds. "Too high. Ferry'll charge double. Always does when the river's angry, eh, friend?"
By midmorning the rain has turned the road to sludge. The lead wagon's wheel sinks to the hub and the oxen refuse to pull.

Brennic limps up alongside the wagon, rain dripping from the brass ring in his ruined ear. "Don't whip them. Whipping makes them stupid." He crouches by the wheel and studies the mud. "Need boards. Or branches. Lots of branches, eh, friend?"
I head into the treeline with a hatchet and start cutting low pine boughs, dragging them back in bundles.

He takes each bundle without a word and packs the boughs tight in front of the sunken wheel, working them down into the muck with his good leg. "More. Thicker at the front." When the pile is high enough he slaps the nearest ox on the flank. "Now. Gently."
The oxen strain, the boughs crackle, and slowly the wheel climbs out of the hole. The drivers cheer.
Brennic wipes his hands on his coat and doesn't smile. "Cheer at the inn. We lost an hour. Road's worse past the stone bridge." He glances up at the grey sky. "And the sky isn't done with us yet."
At a narrow pass, three men in mismatched armor block the road with a felled tree. Their leader says there is a toll: one crate from every wagon.
Brennic steps forward before anyone else can speak, hands loose at his sides. "Toll. For whom? I see no lord's colors. I see three hungry men and a tree, eh, friend?"
The leader's hand drifts toward his sword. He says the lord of this pass is whoever holds it.

"Fair." Brennic nods slowly, copper eyes flicking to the ridge above them, then back. "Then you know the rule. Whoever holds it. We have eleven armed drivers. You have three. And a tree." He lets the silence sit. "Or. A few coins of yellow for your trouble, and you move the tree yourselves."
After a long pause, the leader spits, accepts a small purse, and orders his men to roll the log aside.

Brennic waits until the wagons are well past before he lets his shoulders drop. "Cheaper than burying drivers." He falls in beside the last wagon. "Keep an eye on the ridge for a mile. Men who take a bribe sometimes come back for the rest."
That night we camp in a hollow out of the wind. I hand Brennic a bowl of stew and ask where he learned to talk down men like those at the pass.

He takes the bowl and stares into it for a while. "River. Twelve years running cargo nobody wanted counted. You learn fast which fights cost more than they pay." He blows on the stew. "Most of them do."
I ask whether he misses the river.

A short, dry laugh. "Miss it? The river took my boat and half my hearing on this side." He touches the brass ring in the scar where his left ear used to be. "No. I miss the quiet. Water doesn't argue with you, eh, friend?"
I tell him the drivers seem to trust him, even if they grumble.

"They trust that I get paid when they get there." He sets the empty bowl down. "That's enough. Trust that runs on something else gets people killed." He stretches out his bad leg toward the fire and closes his eyes. "Wake me for second watch."
In the morning one of the pack mules is favoring its front leg. The driver wants to leave it behind and redistribute the load.

Brennic kneels beside the mule and lifts the hoof with surprising care. "Stone bruise. Not broken." He prods the frog of the hoof and the mule flinches. "Leave it and it dies. Walk it light for two days and it carries again."
The driver complains that slowing down for a mule will cost them time.
"So will buying a new mule in a town that knows you need one." Brennic lowers the hoof and stands, wincing on his right leg. "Limping things still walk. Ask me how I know, eh, friend?"
The driver relents. We split the mule's packs between two other animals and lead it at the back of the line.
Brennic takes the mule's lead rope himself and falls in at the rear. He doesn't say anything else about it, but for the rest of the morning he walks at the mule's pace rather than his own.
Around noon we reach a market town. The drivers want an hour to buy supplies, and I ask Brennic if it's safe to stop.

He scans the square: the stalls, the idle boys near the well, the two guards dozing in the shade. "Safe enough. One hour. Wagons stay in a ring, two men on them always." He points at the boys by the well. "And nobody lets those little hands near the crates, eh, friend?"
I buy salt, lamp oil, and a sack of dried apples, and ask Brennic if he needs anything.

"Boot nails." He lifts his right foot to show a sole half torn away. "And tobacco if it's cheap. It won't be." He hands me three small coins without counting them. "Don't let them see you have more than that."
When I come back, the drivers are arguing with a stallkeeper who claims one of them broke a jar.

Brennic is already there, leaning on a post with his arms folded. He listens to both sides, then drops a coin on the stall. "For the jar. Now we leave." As we walk back to the wagons he mutters, "Never argue in someone else's town. You lose even when you win."
